results.claim: THEOREM 2.1(d) 'explicit published instance': Polymath8b prove that, even under GEH, the best a purely sieve-theoretic argument can reach for an admissible triple is 'at least two of n+h_1, n+h_2, n+h_3 are prime', and that this is optimal for sieve-theoretic considerations. The file also quotes the abstract verbatim for the optimality sentence.
results.paper_quote: Abstract (v4): 'for any admissible triple (h_1,h_2,h_3), there are infinitely many n for which at least two of n+h_1,n+h_2,n+h_3 are prime. ... the H_1 <= 6 bound is the best possible that one can obtain from purely sieve-theoretic considerations.' Sec. 8: 'the "parity barrier" of Selberg prohibits sieve-theoretic methods ... from obtaining any bound on H_1 that is stronger than H_1 <= 6, even on the assumption of ... GEH ... and even if one uses sieves other than the Selberg sieve.' Also Theorem 1.4(xii)/3.2(xii): DHL[3,2] under GEH[theta], 0<theta<1.
results.doc_quote: **(d) (explicit published instance.)** Polymath8b prove that, even under the **generalised Elliott–Halberstam conjecture**, the best a purely sieve-theoretic argument can reach for an admissible triple is *"at least two of `n+h_1, n+h_2, n+h_3` are prime"*, and that this is **optimal** for sieve-theoretic considerations.
results.notes: Both halves check out: the admissible-triple statement is verbatim in the v4 abstract and is Theorem 1.4(xii)/DHL[3,2]; optimality is Section 8, which phrases the ceiling as H_1 <= 6. Caveats: (1) the optimality argument is not a numbered theorem and is called 'somewhat informal and heuristic in nature'; it does not assert pointwise counts for every k>=2, so parts (a)-(c) of this file, esp. (c) 'for any admissible tuple with k>=2', generalise the parity principle beyond any numbered Polymath8b result. (2) VERSION: the quoted abstract sentence ('this result is the best possible ...') is verbatim from v1 only; v2-v4 reword it to 'the H_1 <= 6 bound is the best possible'. No version recorded.

results.claim: T8: H_1 = liminf(p_{n+1}-p_n) <= 246; <= 6 under the generalised Elliott-Halberstam conjecture; 'at least two of three' is optimal for purely sieve-theoretic considerations. Cited as THEOREM, Polymath arXiv:1407.4897, Res. Math. Sci. 1:12 (2014), status 'verified (arXiv API: title, journal ref, full abstract)'.
results.paper_quote: Theorem 1.4: '(i) H_1 <= 246' (unconditional); 'Finally, assume the generalized Elliott-Halberstam conjecture GEH[theta] ... (xii) H_1 <= 6'. Abstract: 'we can obtain the bound H_1 <= 246 unconditionally, and H_1 <= 6 under the assumption of the generalized Elliott-Halberstam conjecture ... for any admissible triple (h_1,h_2,h_3), there are infinitely many n for which at least two of n+h_1,n+h_2,n+h_3 are prime'. Intro: 'the parity problem prohibits one from achieving any better bound on H_1 than 6 from purely sieve-theoretic methods.'
results.doc_quote: **T8** — `H_1 = liminf(p_{n+1}−p_n) ≤ 246`; `≤ 6` under the generalised Elliott–Halberstam conjecture; "at least two of three" is optimal for purely sieve-theoretic considerations.
results.notes: All three clauses match the source; arXiv abs page confirms title, sole author D. H. J. Polymath and journal ref 'Research in the Mathematical Sciences 1:12 (2014)'. Hypotheses faithful: the 246 bound is unconditional (and depends only on Bombieri-Vinogradov per the intro), the 6 bound needs GEH[theta] for all 0<theta<1 (the paper notes a single theta close to 1 suffices). Minor: the archive's quoted words 'at least two of three' are its own shorthand, not a paper phrase; and the row does not record which arXiv version was verified (the abstract wording changed between v1 and v2-v4).
